messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi's eyes still widened when he recalled the night he was stopped by police on his way home from a late meeting with colleagues. It had been a routine traffic stop, but the officer's tone and mannerisms had escalated the situation, leaving Kofi shaken. The memory of being ordered out of his car, hands raised, while his wife watched from the passenger seat, still felt like an open wound. When it resurfaced, as it often did in the months that followed, Kofi felt overwhelmed by a mix of emotions: fear, anger, and helplessness. He would have to stop whatever he was doing – whether working on a curriculum design project or helping his kids with homework – and collect himself before he could continue. As time passed, Kofi found it increasingly difficult to articulate what had happened that night. The details seemed to slip away from him like sand between his fingers. When he tried to recount the events to friends or family, he would become frustrated by his inability to put the experience into words. His wife, Nana, would often finish his sentences for him, as if trying to fill in the gaps. But even with her support, Kofi felt like a part of him was frozen in time. Physical reactions became more common, too. When he heard sirens or saw police cars on the road, his heart rate would spike, and his palms would grow sweaty. He began to notice how jumpy he had become – how easily startled by sudden noises or movements. His kids would tease him about being "on edge" all the time, but Kofi knew it wasn't just a joke. He felt like he was constantly on guard, waiting for something else to go wrong. As a curriculum designer, Kofi's work required him to be creative and focused. But since the incident, he had found himself increasingly preoccupied with thoughts of safety and security. He would get caught up in hypothetical scenarios – what if this happened, or that? – and before long, his mind would wander back to that fateful night. His colleagues began to notice a change in him; meetings would pass without Kofi contributing much, as he was lost in thought. Nana noticed the changes too, of course. She would try to reassure him, reminding him that they were safe now, but Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling of vulnerability. At times, he felt like he was drowning in emotions without being able to recall the exact events that had triggered them. His family life began to suffer as a result; dinner conversations grew strained, and plans for weekend outings were cancelled due to Kofi's anxiety. One evening, as they sat down for dinner, their daughter asked why Dad seemed so "sad" all the time. Nana tried to explain, but Kofi knew he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this – constantly on edge, unable to shake off the memories of that night. The realization hit him: it was time to seek professional help, not just for himself, but for his family's sake as well.
